# Computing {#computing}

The lab's computing stack is built around reproducibility and openness. Everything we produce — code, data, analyses — lives in version control from day one.

---

## Why it matters {#why-computing}

### Open & transparent science {#open-science}

We pre-register study designs, share code and data publicly, and archive null results alongside positive ones. This isn't overhead — it's how we make our science trustworthy and durable.

- **Pre-registration:** Register your study design on [OSF](https://osf.io) *before* data collection. This protects against unconscious p-hacking and signals scientific integrity to reviewers.
- **Public code:** All analysis code is published in the lab GitHub org at or before paper submission. Comment your code as if someone else will run it — because they will.
- **Data archiving:** Raw data are archived in a domain repository (e.g., NCBI, BCO-DMO, OSF) at publication. Never publish a paper without a data availability statement that works.
- **Null results:** Experiments that don't go as planned are still science. Document and report them internally at minimum; consider a registered report or null result publication.

### Lab computing stack {#stack}

| Tool | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Bash / Linux** | Navigation, file management, scripting, HPC job submission |
| **Git & GitHub** | Version control for all code and documentation |
| **R & RStudio** | Statistical analysis, visualization, bioinformatics |
| **HPC cluster** | Large-scale computation — genomics, environmental modeling |
| **Discord** | Lab communication; `#computing-help` for technical questions |
| **OSF** | Pre-registration, data archiving, supplementary materials |

## Linux & Bash {#bash}

### Introduction {#bash-intro}

The command line gives you direct, scriptable control over your files, data, and compute jobs. Everything you do on the HPC will be in Bash. Even locally, it is faster and more reproducible than point-and-click.

Open a terminal:

- **macOS:** Applications → Utilities → Terminal (or install [iTerm2](https://iterm2.com))
- **Windows:** Install [Git Bash](https://git-scm.com/downloads) or use WSL
- **Linux:** Already have one

### Navigating directories {#bash-navigate}

```bash
pwd           # print working directory — where am I?
ls            # list files in current directory
ls -lh        # list with details and human-readable sizes
ls -a         # include hidden files (dotfiles)
cd Documents  # change into the Documents folder
cd ..         # go up one level
cd ~          # go to your home directory
cd -          # go back to the previous directory
```

### Reading & editing files {#bash-files}

```bash
cat file.txt          # print entire file
head -20 file.txt     # first 20 lines
tail -20 file.txt     # last 20 lines
less file.txt         # scroll through (q to quit)

nano file.txt         # simple editor — good for quick edits
vim file.txt          # powerful editor — press i to insert, Esc then :wq to save and quit
```

### Moving & copying files {#bash-move}

```bash
cp file.txt backup.txt          # copy file
cp -r folder/ folder_backup/    # copy a whole directory
mv file.txt new_name.txt        # rename
mv file.txt ../other_folder/    # move to another folder
```

### Deleting files {#bash-delete}

```bash
rm file.txt           # delete a file (no recycle bin — permanent)
rm -r folder/         # delete a folder and all its contents
```

<div class="callout-warn">
`rm` is permanent. There is no undo, no recycle bin. Double-check before you run it, especially with wildcards. `rm -rf /` or `rm -rf *` can wipe your entire system.
</div>

### Wildcards {#bash-wildcards}

```bash
ls *.csv              # list all .csv files
cp data_*.txt backup/ # copy all files matching the pattern
rm temp_*.log         # delete all matching log files
```

### Practice exercise {#bash-practice}

```bash
mkdir bash_practice
cd bash_practice
echo "Hello GurrLab" > hello.txt
cat hello.txt
cp hello.txt hello_copy.txt
ls -lh
rm hello_copy.txt
cd ..
```

## Git & GitHub {#git}

### Overview {#git-overview}

**Git** is a version control system — it tracks changes to files so you can see history, revert mistakes, and collaborate without overwriting each other's work.

**GitHub** is a website that hosts Git repositories. It adds collaboration features: pull requests, issues, project boards, and GitHub Pages.

Think of Git as the engine and GitHub as the garage where you store and share your work.

### Setup & SSH {#git-setup}

```bash
# Set your identity (do this once)
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@oregonstate.edu"
git config --global core.editor "nano"  # or vim

# Generate an SSH key so you don't need to type your password
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@oregonstate.edu"
# Press Enter to accept defaults

# Copy the public key
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
# Paste it into GitHub → Settings → SSH and GPG keys → New SSH key
```

### Clone a repository {#git-clone}

```bash
# Clone a repo from GitHub to your local machine
git clone git@github.com:GurrLab/your-repo.git
cd your-repo
```

### Daily workflow {#daily-workflow}

```bash
git pull                        # get latest changes from GitHub
# ... make your edits ...
git status                      # see what has changed
git add analysis.R              # stage a specific file
git add .                       # stage all changed files
git commit -m "Add CO2 analysis script"   # commit with a message
git push                        # push to GitHub
```

**Commit message tips:**

- Use the imperative mood: *"Add..."*, *"Fix..."*, *"Update..."* not *"Added..."*
- Be specific: `"Fix salinity calibration in water_chem.R"` not `"fix bug"`
- Commit small and often — don't wait until the end of the day

### Branches & pull requests {#git-branches}

```bash
git checkout -b feature/new-analysis   # create and switch to a new branch
# ... make changes ...
git add .
git commit -m "Add new analysis approach"
git push -u origin feature/new-analysis
```

Then on GitHub: open a **Pull Request** from your branch into `main`. Request a review from your collaborator. Merge after review.

### Merge conflicts {#git-conflicts}

A merge conflict happens when two people edit the same line in the same file. Git marks the conflict like this:

```
<<<<<<< HEAD
result <- model_a(data)
=======
result <- model_b(data)
>>>>>>> feature/new-analysis
```

Resolve it by editing the file to keep what you want, removing the markers, then:

```bash
git add conflicted_file.R
git commit -m "Resolve merge conflict in analysis"
```

### New repository checklist {#git-new-repo}

When starting any new project:

- [ ] Create the repo in the [GurrLab GitHub org](https://github.com/GurrLab) (not your personal account)
- [ ] Add a `README.md` describing the project, data sources, and how to run the code
- [ ] Add a `.gitignore` appropriate for your language (R, Python)
- [ ] Make the repo **public** unless there is a specific reason not to
- [ ] Never commit raw data files > 50 MB — use OSF or the lab NAS for large files

## R & RStudio {#r}

### Getting started {#r-setup}

Download and install in this order:

1. [R](https://cran.r-project.org) — the language
2. [RStudio](https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/) — the IDE

Core packages to install immediately:

```r
install.packages(c(
  "tidyverse",   # data wrangling and visualization
  "here",        # reproducible file paths
  "rmarkdown",   # reproducible reports
  "devtools"     # installing packages from GitHub
))
```

### Reproducible project structure {#r-structure}

Use RStudio Projects (`.Rproj`) for every analysis. Never use `setwd()`.

```
my_project/
├── data/
│   ├── raw/          # never modify these
│   └── processed/
├── R/                # scripts and functions
├── output/
│   ├── figures/
│   └── tables/
├── docs/             # manuscripts, notes
└── README.md
```

Use `here::here()` to build file paths:

```r
library(here)
data <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "samples.csv"))
```

## HPC cluster {#hpc}

The OSU HPC (High Performance Computing) cluster is where you run large jobs — genome assembly, environmental modeling, permutation tests with thousands of iterations.

### Getting an account {#hpc-account}

Request an account through [HPC documentation — link TBD]. Copy the PI on your request email.

### Connecting {#hpc-connect}

```bash
ssh your_onid@submit.hpc.oregonstate.edu
```

### Submitting a job (SLURM) {#hpc-slurm}

```bash
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=my_analysis
#SBATCH --output=logs/job_%j.out
#SBATCH --error=logs/job_%j.err
#SBATCH --time=04:00:00
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=8
#SBATCH --mem=32G
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL
#SBATCH --mail-user=you@oregonstate.edu

module load R/4.3.0
Rscript analysis.R
```

Submit with `sbatch job.sh`. Monitor with `squeue -u your_onid`.

### Good HPC habits {#hpc-habits}

- Test on a small dataset locally before submitting large jobs
- Use `--time` conservatively — overestimate to avoid job termination
- Clean up `/scratch` after jobs complete (scratch is not backed up)
- Document your software versions with `module list` in your job script output
